title: Why is the U.S. so dependent on cars?
summary: Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant discuss why the United States became so dependent on cars. They open with local Atlanta transit debates (Marta, the Atlanta belt line, and a proposed rail line opposed by officials and residents, plus the plan to widen I-75). They trace early street rail lines in New York and New Orleans, the German origins of the automobile (Daimler, Benz, the Mercedes name), and Henry Ford's assembly line and Model T. They cover the role of railways in opening the country, and the decline of trolleys and streetcars, including the National City Lines scandal (GM, Firestone, Standard Oil of California, Phillips Petroleum), the 1949 antitrust case with its one-dollar fine, and Bradford Snell's 1974 Senate testimony. They discuss ethanol versus gasoline as fuel, the Interstate Highway Act under Eisenhower, zoning and parking requirements, roadside business, and the Cash for Clunkers program. The episode closes with listener mail urging blood and platelet donation.

segments.title: Opening banter and Atlanta transit debate
segments.summary: The hosts chat about their commutes, then discuss an Atlanta rail proposal opposed by local officials, the argument that transit increases crime, and the claim that widening roads does not relieve congestion. They introduce the article by John Fuller.

segments.title: Car-centered design and early street rail
segments.summary: They note how cities, malls and parking lots are built around cars and mention the Atlanta belt line. They then cover the 1832 New York and New Orleans horse-drawn street rail lines.

segments.title: Origins of the automobile and Henry Ford
segments.summary: Gottlieb Daimler is described as a first developer of a functioning automobile, and the car was named after his daughter Mercedes. Daimler partnered with Carl Benz. Henry Ford is credited with perfecting the car by applying the assembly line, which he did not invent. Ford's company built about 14 million Model Ts between 1913 and 1927. Early cars were considered a plaything of the rich and were called stink chariots.

segments.title: Railroads and the opening of the country
segments.summary: Before railroads, overland travel was hard without roads. Railways opened the continent and were heavily used, with about 1.2 billion riders a year at peak. Rail was good for long distances but less convenient for commuting.

segments.title: Car adoption and the rise of cars over rail
segments.summary: Cars became cheaper and gave people control over their schedules, privacy and freedom. The hosts mention road rage and subway rage, including the Marta rant by a woman known as Soldier Girl. They discuss trolleys in Los Angeles and other cities.

segments.title: National City Lines and the streetcar scandal
segments.summary: National City Lines was formed by about eight companies including General Motors, Firestone, Standard Oil of California and Phillips Petroleum to buy streetcar systems and replace them with buses. E. J. Quinby, a former trolley manager, wrote letters alerting officials. The company was indicted under antitrust law and acquitted of monopolizing ground transportation but found guilty of monopolizing bus sales, fined one dollar. Bradford Snell testified before the Senate in 1974, renewing public attention. The hosts note the motive is disputed, though the outcome was the same.

segments.title: Ethanol versus gasoline and the Interstate Highway Act
segments.summary: Henry Ford designed the Model T to run on gasoline or ethanol and promoted ethanol as the fuel of the future. Gasoline won because cheap oil from Texas fields made it less expensive. President Eisenhower signed the Interstate Highway Act, and the hosts discuss how highways and car-oriented zoning, including parking requirements and businesses pushed away from sidewalks, shaped the economy.

segments.title: Conclusion, car economics and Cash for Clunkers
segments.summary: The hosts note that transit is making a comeback as gas prices rise but is unlikely to overtake cars. They mention the Cash for Clunkers program, which sold a quarter million cars with the first billion dollars, and they summarize why cars became dominant: they were cheaper at the right time and consumers wanted them. They point listeners to the website for links.

segments.title: Website and webcast plugs
segments.summary: The hosts plug the shared blog and the weekly webcast.
